rows: My argument has two parts. The second only matters if you can answer the first.
Brawling is a conduct question before it is a wrestling one. Let me state the standard.
A gamble is a premise. Its conclusion is the outcome, and the premise must be stated first.
Pace is part of the framework. It should be agreed before it is changed.
The people are the audience to whom the standard applies. I will state it clearly for them.
The standard is stated, and I invite scrutiny of it.
I have a standard of conduct, and I intend to keep to it in public.
Watch the stance. It is the position the argument requires.
Technique is premise one. State the first premise: what does the hold require? Then we can judge it.
Strikes are permitted within the stated framework. Outside it, they are not.
A gamble taken without a stated premise cannot be assessed. State yours.
A stall is an argument that has run out of premises. I will not accept it.
The people deserve a contest judged against a stated standard. I will provide one.
You say I am out of place. Test that claim against the standard, and then we will see.
You are proud of your {strength}. Good. State the premise it rests on. Fine. State the premise it rests on, and I will reply to that premise.
I have tested your {strength} against the standard, and it fails on one premise.
You stayed level, premise two. Fine. Calm allows the argument to be followed.
That is a fair premise. That premise is sound, and I accept it.
I could dispute that in several ways. I will dispute only the one that matters.
One fall, the conclusion. Those are the terms of the conclusion. Meet them, and the result stands.
On the mat, the framework remains as stated. Work within it.
Grounded or standing, the framework does not shift.
Stay in front of me and answer the argument in full.
Decent answer. It follows from the premise.
No answer yet. The argument requires your reply.
That is a fair premise. That point is on the record.
I accept that premise. We will test the conclusion at the bell.
I will wrestle this match within the stated framework, and I will reach the conclusion honestly.
My approach is structured. You will see the framework on the night.
Whatever happens, the record will show the argument as it was made.
The argument is not closed. One premise is still open.
I have one more premise to state, and you will hear it when the bell rings.
Your objection is sound. I have offered a conclusion without establishing its premise. I withdraw it.
There is no specific evidence I can offer to support the charge. The argument cannot proceed on that basis.
Then we can discard that premise and retain the sporting question.
Accepted. We have established the limit of that argument. The match remains to be decided.
The test is observable conduct within the agreed rules, followed by an official result. That is the limit of the conclusion.
We can examine the method as well as the result. Neither establishes a separate allegation without separate evidence.
Let us separate the allegation from the evidence of the contest. What conclusion can the latter support?
We should agree on the standard before the bell. What can the people observe that meets it?
Your proposed answer to my {strength} rests on the premise that I accept the position you require. I do not.
You have identified my {strength}. The conclusion you draw must still be tested within the stated rules of the contest.
That is a sound premise. The allegation requires evidence before it supports a conclusion.
I accept that distinction. The contest can establish a result, not the truth of every assertion.
The premise that experience is valuable is sound. The conclusion that it decides this match does not follow.
Your years in wrestling are relevant to your preparation. The standard of the contest remains the same for both of us.
Repeated practice helps distinguish a familiar position from one that merely resembles it.
Experience is useful because it gives me grounds to revise a decision when the original premise fails.
Your research establishes a premise. It does not demonstrate that your proposed response will succeed.
You have studied my previous decisions. What grounds do you have for assuming that the circumstances will be identical?
I study the evidence for and against each likely response, then test the distinction in practice.
I prepare by identifying the assumptions a technique depends on and rehearsing what to do when one fails.
